Integer Rectangles: A Proof by Induction

InvariantsAlgorithmsLogic
Game: Shrink a tiled rectangle step by step until its integer side is forced.
How to play: Split the tiles, select a green one, then Extend, Remove path and Close gap. Induct does the whole run.

Look for the math

One of the shortest proofs of the rectangle tiling theorem uses nothing but repeated shrinking.

Split and shrink

First split each green H-tile into unit-width strips and each red V-tile into unit-height strips. Pick a green tile and extend it through the ones stacked above and below it until a column reaches from the bottom edge to the top. Remove that column and slide the right-hand part one unit left: the new rectangle has fewer green tiles, and any integer side it has is an integer side of the original.

The base case

With no green tiles left, only unit-height red tiles remain. They must stack from bottom to top, so the height is a whole number. That finishes the induction. The logic test checks the split, the column search, each shrink and the base case on Winkler's tiling.

The same shrink can be applied to a row. If both sides of the big rectangle were non-integer, repeatedly reducing the longer side by one would eventually leave a rectangle with both sides under one — which cannot be tiled at all. That is the page's additional proof #15.5.

Press Split, then Extend on a green tile. What happens to the red tiles when you close the gap?
